clips.title: How to use GitHub Actions | GitHub for Beginners
clips.why: Two people from GitHub explain in two minutes what Actions is for, before we read any YAML.
look: The idea of automation that reacts to something happening in the repo: that something is the event.
How continuous integration fits in: a machine tests every change, so nobody has to remember to run the tests.
The words they use for the parts, so you can match them to event, workflow, job and step.
clips.after: Every check on an fcp pull request, including Nova's, is this kind of automation, started by a push or a PR event.

clips.title: Github Actions CI/CD - Everything you need to know to get started
clips.why: A short walk through one workflow file, top to bottom, which is exactly how you should read frontend-ci.yaml.
look: Where the file lives: .github/workflows in the repo.
The on: block first, then jobs, then the steps inside a job.
Which steps are shell commands (run) and which are published actions (uses).
clips.after: Read fcp's frontend-ci.yaml in the same order: name, on, permissions, jobs, and you can explain every check on a PR.

clips.title: GitHub Actions Tutorial - Basic Concepts and CI/CD Pipeline with Docker
clips.why: Nana answers the question from our story: where does the workflow's code actually run?
look: Each job gets its own runner, a fresh machine, which is why files do not cross between jobs.
Jobs run in parallel by default, and needs makes one wait for another.
GitHub-hosted runners versus runners you host yourself, like our fcp-runner-set.
clips.after: The summary job failed because it ran on a second machine; fcp-runner-set gives every job a fresh container in our own cluster in the same way.

clips.title: GitHub Actions: GITHUB_TOKEN Explained | How it works, Change Permissions, Customizations
clips.why: A focused explanation of the token every job gets, and how the permissions block limits it.
look: The token is created for the job and expires with it, so there is no secret to manage.
The difference between GITHUB_TOKEN and a personal access token.
Setting permissions per scope, and what happens to the scopes you leave out.
clips.after: Our workflows set a permissions block every time, so a job can do only what its one task needs.

practice.q: You push a commit to a branch with an open PR. Put what happens in order.
items: GitHub records a pull_request event for the new commit
GitHub reads every file in .github/workflows and finds the ones whose on: block matches
Each matching workflow starts a run, and each of its jobs gets a fresh runner
The steps of each job run in order, and a failing step stops that job
Each job reports its result, which the PR shows as a check
practice.why: The event comes first, the on: block decides which workflows care, and only then do machines start. The check you see on the PR is the job's result, named after the job.

practice.q: The build job writes dist/app.js. The deploy job, with needs: build, must upload that file. What is the right way to hand it over?

options.text: Nothing extra: needs: build makes the folder available to deploy
options.why: needs only orders the jobs. deploy still starts on a fresh runner with an empty folder.

options.text: Upload it as an artifact in build and download it in deploy
options.why: An artifact is a file GitHub stores with the run, so the next job can fetch it onto its own machine.

options.text: Write the whole file into $GITHUB_OUTPUT and read it in deploy
options.why: Outputs are for short strings, like a count or a version. A built file belongs in an artifact.

practice.q: The summary job has needs: unit-tests. Finish the expression that reads the tests output of the unit-tests job.
practice.hint: It is the same word as the key that makes summary wait for unit-tests.
practice.why: A job reads another job's outputs through needs.<job>.outputs.<name>, and only for jobs it lists under needs.

practice.q: A step must publish the value tests=412 so that the job's outputs block can read it. Finish the line.
practice.hint: GitHub puts the path of a special file in an environment variable; you append name=value lines to it.
practice.why: Writing name=value into the file at $GITHUB_OUTPUT is how a step publishes a value as steps.<id>.outputs.<name>.

practice.q: A new workflow only clones the repo and runs the linter. Which permissions block fits?

options.text: No permissions block, so the repository default applies
options.why: The default can be write on almost everything. Without a block you cannot tell from the file what the job is allowed to do.

options.text: permissions: write-all, so the linter never hits a 403
options.why: That hands a linter the power to push code and change PRs. Give the least that works.
Reading the repo is all a clone needs. Every scope you do not list becomes none.

practice.q: actionlint says: label "fcp-runner-set" is unknown. What do you do?

options.text: Change runs-on to ubuntu-latest so actionlint is happy
options.why: That would move the job off our runners, which can reach internal services. The label is right; actionlint just does not know it.

options.text: List fcp-runner-set under self-hosted-runner labels in .github/actionlint.yaml
options.why: actionlint only knows GitHub's own labels. Our own runner labels go in its config file, as fcp already does.

options.text: Ignore it, because actionlint warnings never matter
options.why: Most actionlint findings are real mistakes. This one is a missing config line, so fix the config instead of ignoring the tool.
